rv.q: But with its exuberance, heart and non-stop yucks, “Shucked” is the surprise delight of the season.
If you’re fond of laughing, “Shucked” is the best new musical of the Broadway season so far.
The show is unabashedly corny, but it's also genuinely funny and surprisingly well-crafted.
And snorts, giggles and rolled eyes are what it delivers.
This corny musical about corn farmers is both aggressively silly and surprisingly sweet.
With its gentle digs at small-town closed-mindedness, it might end up working best in the blue-voting urban precincts of red states.
The musical's appeal lies in its commitment to the ridiculous, its willingness to lean into the corniest possible jokes about corn and small-town life.
The thing is defiantly irreducible, because its aims are simple and direct.
Embrace each grain of fun and you’ll have an amazing night on Broadway.
About one-third of the jokes land — and most come out of nowhere, having nothing to do with the story or its characters.
Like Gordy, the audience may have difficulty extracting the gems from the corn.
I'm not the buyer of this particular variety, but corn sells – which, in the name of an original musical, is something to root for.
Before you know it, you're gorged to satisfaction on a big, tasty bag of Broadway puff.
It’s all about laughs, and it delivers – honest to cob.
The pleasure of watching Shucked is not only that it's very funny, it is also a musical comedy comfortable in its merry skin
Shucked is about as quick and easy a good time can be had on Broadway: accessible, unpretentious and, I’ll be damned, a whole lot of fun.

Add in an appealing, occasionally rowdy country-inflected score by the Grammy-winning songwriting team of Brandy Clark and Shane McAnally, and you've got yourself a show that is both whimsically hokey and welcoming as an old friend.
Let’s just go with an endearing, soil-kicking “Aw, shucks!”

The musical, featuring a book by Robert Horn (Tootsie) and songs by Nashville veterans Brandy Clark and Shane McAnally, emerges as one of the brightest surprises of the spring season, delivering more hilarious gags per minute than any show since The Book of Mormon.
Shucked is a corny musical that knows it's corny and revels in that corniness with such infectious enthusiasm that you can't help but get swept up in its amber waves of grain.
Even if you're not in the mood for some feel-good sentiment, as a laugh-out-loud crowd-pleaser, 'Shucked' is a shucking good time.
For those seeking a lighter form of diversion, though, the corn here is undeniably fresh, sweet, and juicy.
Much like the experience of eating corn, Shucked is kind of great.
When all’s said and done, Shucked is exactly as much fun as you’ll let it be.
It's too soon to tell if Shucked has staying power as a Broadway musical, but its refreshing embrace of diversity and unapologetically corny sincerity can definitely put a smile on your face.
Maybe not, but it definitely provides more of a window than a wall.

One could try to read into it as a parable of community, commitment, tolerance, and so on, but “Shucked” is really just a lightweight and laborious attempt at resurrecting old-fashioned musical comedy with a country flavor and corn as high as an elephant’s eye.
Shorn from its earwormy songs and bubbly ensemble, Shucked tends to fade.
That often funny and occasionally exhausting new musical makes Shucked seem a lot longer than its two and twenty minutes.
"Shucked" is, simply put, arguably the funniest comedy I have ever seen in a theater.
As long as New York audiences—many themselves from rural places—don’t mind too much hick in their shtick, Shucked should keep Broadway laughing till the cows come home.
Shucked is an absolute delight.
What makes SHUCKED so irresistibly appealing even to the most cynical of theatregoers is its sly, self-aware humor wrapped around a sincere emotional core.
Most importantly, it is loads of fun.
'Shucked' offers a refreshing reminder of our shared humanity and the power of community.

Go see Shucked, you’ll laugh, a lot, at the wonderful wit, you’ll join in the jubilation as the whole audience elatedly exclaims together as the corn visibly comes back to life, and you’ll maybe even shed a tear.
But it will cause you to have a big smile on your face – and nothing in your teeth – for two hours.
Shucked weaves together a thoroughly enjoyable theatrical experience, juxtaposing immature puns with songs that actually have a lot to say.

I know these are some of the darkest and most dangerous days in our lifetimes. With despair and desperation haunting so many people on the planet, thank the powers that be for letting us forget all that for a couple of hours and wallow in the shallows of some good old fashioned corn porn. A delightful fantasy that has laughs galore, lots of corny jokes, and wonderful characters.
Shucked isn't here to change the world or unlock any deeper truths. But for two and a half hours, it'll make you laugh, maybe cry, definitely tap your toes.
Aw shucks, you really should experience this play on your own.
I'd be lying if I didn't admit to laughing a good seventy-five percent of the time.

The story is a fairly simple one, but its clever and witty banter gave it a fun freshness. Amid its country music soundtrack, its endless array of corn puns and dad jokes and its rom-com cuteness, Robert Horn’s book and Brandy Clark and Shane McAnally’s music and lyrics blend into a satisfying musical experience with a big heart.
The entire cast truly shines, from the ensemble to the leading lady.
You have seen this plot before but the spectacular voices, great humor, and message about love offer a joyous and hopeful respite from the challenges of the real world.

It asks nothing more from its audience than to sit back and enjoy. And isn't that enough?
Shucked offers the Broadway equivalent of a solid popcorn flick: an escapist romp through a maze of love, laughs and corn.
You won’t like “Shucked” if you can’t get a little corny with it.
If they happen to be looking for a tight, well written Broadway musical with substance and pay full price for a ticket, they may feel they've been 'Shucked.'

By the second act of "Shucked," the constant jokes harvest as many groans as giggles. All the jokes are good though. While the constant quips with a pause for laughter wore me out, the rows were still full after the second act. The crowd yukked it up until the end.
I had a brainlessly good time I can scarcely remember two hours later, as I write this.
Otherwise, you might find yourself bored or exasperated.

But that style of Americana vaudeville depends on a certain tone and timing, which this show only intermittently achieved for me during its two-and-a-half-hour run.
